about: The words of the chain house_marriage (encounters/chain_house_marriage_793.json; the page is Design/content/chains/house_marriage.md), written 4 Oct 2026: a draft for the user to overwrite. Keys are ch_house_marriage.<step>.<line>; the picture for each card is art.<card id>. No line names its speaker, because the engine's forge names the people. Where a line follows a text closely it carries a 'source'; the one quotation is ch_house_marriage.s08.verse (Thorpe 1842, free to use).

entries.text: An empty house
The widow who keeps the storehouse on the dam stops you at the dam head. She says a house with one man in it is not a house, and offers to ask about a wife for you.
Your father's house has a boat, a bed and one man in it. Who keeps your keys while you are at sea? I looked. Nobody does.
You still owe the count. A bride's father minds that less than you think, if you pay on the day. He watches the day, not the purse.
You owe the count nothing now. To a bride's father that is worth more than a new cloak.
I know who has daughters between here and the Danes, and what each house is short of. Shall I ask? It costs you nothing but being talked about.
I ask because I would rather lend to a house than to a boat. A boat can sink in an afternoon.
Let her ask
Give her twelve pennies to ask properly
Not this year
Four houses
The widow has asked on the dams and among the ships. Four houses would hear a suitor from Dorestad: a Frisian, a Frankish, an English and a Danish one. Each wants something that is not silver.
I have asked. Four houses would hear you. None is cheap, and each wants something besides the price.

Winaldum, on the mounds past the Almere. A free farmer with sheep, a boat, and a daughter who weaves the cloth the Franks pay for. Her mother's brother must agree; among us he always must. They want wine, and a man who comes back.

Traiectum. The bishop's steward has a daughter. He holds his plot of Saint Martin, so the bishop must give leave, and a priest will ask after your kin to the fourth knee. They want it all written down.

Eoforwic. This one is my own business, and I will tell you all of it if you choose it. A dead man's daughter, an uncle who holds her hand, and a market shut to every Frisian. A marriage might end what silver never has.
I will not send you blind. They may show you the door, or a blade. But no market in the north is richer.

Ripa. The Dane who answers for our ships there has a daughter and no use for priests. With them a bargain is a handclasp before witnesses, and the price is weighed, not counted. Her gods go where she goes. Your priest will have something to say.

You paid me to ask properly, so: the Frisian uncle's wife grinds on a worn-out stone. The steward's daughter can read. The Englishman's niece has waited all her life to be told the truth. And the Dane's girl weighs her father's silver. She will know what yours weighs.
Go to Winaldum, to the Frisian house
Go to Traiectum, to the steward's house
Go to Eoforwic, to the dead man's kin
Go to Ripa, to the Danish host's house
Who speaks for you
A suitor does not ask for himself. Someone must say he will keep her as a wife should be kept, and go surety for it. The widow offers her word and half a tally; the priest offers a letter.
A man who asks for himself is thought to have no friends. Someone must say you will keep her properly, and stand surety that you will.

Hear it all, then. Years ago at Eoforwic my husband killed a nobleman's son in a brawl. Every Frisian in the city took ship that week. The blood-price was never paid. The dead man's daughter was born after. That is who you are asking for.
I can send my word ahead with the next ship, and give you half a tally to carry. They will have the other half. My name is good on the mounds and at Traiectum.
At Eoforwic my name is the worst you could carry. It is also the only honest one. Think before you show them my tally.
At Ripa nobody has heard of me. They know your host, and they know silver. Take my tally if you like. It will do no harm.
I can write to the priest there that you are baptised, free and unmarried, and no kin of hers within the forbidden knees so far as anyone here knows. A letter is believed where a merchant is not.
To Ripa? They would wrap fish in it. Have it if you wish. I will also pray for you; that they cannot wrap fish in.
Carry the widow's half-tally
Give twelve pennies to the church and carry the priest's letter
Speak for yourself
The crew has heard
Word of the match is aboard before you are. The men have opinions, and the steersman knows something of the people you are going to.
So the boat is to fetch a bride. The men want to know two things. Is she heavy, and does her father brew.
Mound people. They will count your sheep before your silver, and you have no sheep.
A steward's daughter. Then everything will be written down, and read back to you later.
Eoforwic. I knew the boy who was on the ship that left there in a hurry. Nobody knew him better. I will take you up the river. I will not go ashore, and you will not say my name.
Danes. They will be polite. You will not know what it cost you until you are home.
And if the house is getting a wife, the men say the house can stand them a cask.
Ask the steersman what else he knows
Stand them a cask of ale and listen
Tell them to mind the oars
The mound at Winaldum

Her father receives you on the house mound, above the salt marsh. Her mother's brother sits beside him and has not spoken yet. The daughter is at the loom in the sunken hut, and the shuttle has stopped.
You are the one from the dam at Dorestad. Sit. You have come a long way across the Almere to look at sheep.
The widow's word came with the last ship. She says you pay what you owe and come back when you say you will. From her that is a long speech.
A letter. Nobody on this mound reads. But the wax on it is good wax, and a priest does not seal a lie for twelve pennies. We take it as meant.
Nobody speaks for you. Either you have no friends or you are in a hurry. Which?
The law is short. Who takes a free woman without the will of those who keep her pays twenty shillings to her keeper. So we are asked first. I am her mother's brother. I am the one you ask.

A pound of pennies to her father, counted on this mound before her kin. A gift to her on the morning after, which is hers alone. And my wife grinds our corn on a stone her grandmother wore hollow. I mention it for no reason.
If he wants to know what the cloth is worth, he can ask the one who weaves it.
The steersman's advice comes back to you: do not praise the daughter. Praise the cloth, and ask what it sells for. They will hear the rest.
Go to the loom and ask her what the cloth sells for
Lay the widow's half-tally in the father's hand
Promise the uncle black stones from the Rhine
Ask plainly and offer the pound
The steward's table
Inside the old stone fort at Traiectum the bishop's steward hears you at his own table. A priest sits by with a wax tablet, to ask after your kin. The daughter pours the ale and stays to listen.
You are the Frisian with the small boat. I have seen your name on the wrong side of the count's tally. Sit down. A debt paid on the day tells me more than a letter would.
The widow on the dam stands for you. She lent to this house in a bad year and was paid. Her word is taken here.
Your priest's letter says baptised, free, unmarried. That spares us a month of asking up and down the river.
Nobody speaks for you. Then you will swear it yourself, with men beside you, and that takes time to arrange.

Now your kin. Your father, his father, and his. Your mother's side the same. And who lifted you from the font. If your people and hers meet inside the fourth knee, or at the font, there is nothing more to say.
The emperor's order is new, but the rule is old: nobody weds until the priests and the elders of the people have asked into the blood.
entries.source: after the Capitulary of 802 c. 35 (tr. E. F. Henderson 1896)

entries.text: My terms. A dower in writing, read out before witnesses: it is hers if you die first. The wedding in the open, as the king's law asks of noble and common alike. And the bishop's leave, because I hold my plot of Saint Martin, and so does she.
I will read the deed myself, father. Then nobody need wonder later what the clerk left out.
The steersman's advice comes back to you: wash first, and take wax for the church. A steward notices wax.
Hand the priest your letter
Lay two cakes of wax on the table for Saint Martin's altar
Ask the daughter what a dower should hold
Name your kin and let them ask at Dorestad
The dead man's brother

At Eoforwic a Frisian hull is looked at twice. The man who holds the girl's hand is brother to the youth killed in the year the Frisians ran. He hears you standing, a monk beside him to see it done properly, and the niece at the back of the hall among the women.
A Frisian, asking for a woman of my house. My brother was killed by a Frisian on this strand when I was a boy. Say what you want, and who sent you.
The king took a Mercian wife, to make a friend of Offa. So I am told that marriages mend things. My brother has been dead these many winters and nothing has mended.
The blood-price was paid before witnesses and I gave my hand on it. So I hear you as I would hear any man. That is all it bought you.
Nobody has paid for him. Remember it while you talk.

By the old law of the Kentish kings a maiden is bought with cattle, and the bargain stands if there is no guile in it. If there is guile, she is brought home again and he has his cattle back. We say much the same here, in more words.
He carries a priest's letter from over the water: baptised, free, unmarried. The archbishop's people will want that known before anything else is.
The niece has not been asked to speak. She has moved three places nearer the fire since you began.
The steersman's words come back to you: he will not go ashore, and you will not say his name. Someone on this strand will know his face all the same. A thing told is lighter than a thing found.
Show the widow's tally and say whose house stands behind you
Say you are a merchant of Dorestad, and no more
Ask the monk to lay it before the archbishop's man first
The host's fire at Ripa

The Dane who answers for Frisian ships at Ripa hears you by his own fire. His daughter is at the door with the scales, weighing the day's silver. An old woman has been sent for, to ask by lot whether the luck of the house leaves with the girl.

You are from the dam at Dorestad. Your people have lain at my landing since my father's day and paid what guests pay. Now one of you asks for something I do not sell. Speak. I am listening, and so is the door.
He says it slowly, in the few Frisian words a host needs. The daughter laughs at one of yours and does not say which.
Sigfred is king, and he has not said whom a free man's daughter may marry. So it is my business, and her brothers', and the gods'.

With us it goes so. You name the bride-price. I name what she takes from home. We clasp hands on it before witnesses. Within the year the ale is drunk, and six men see you to her bed, so that nobody can say later it was not a marriage.
Two marks of silver. Weighed. I do not know your king's face, and my scales do not need to.
I cut three twigs from a tree that bears, and mark them. I do not ask whether he is a good man. I ask whether the luck stays.
One thing more. She keeps her gods. If your priests wash her, I will hear of it, and you will not lie at my landing again.
The steersman's advice comes back to you: do not haggle over her, or they will think you are buying a cow and sell you one. Let the girl weigh your silver herself. She will anyway.
Put your purse on her scale and say nothing
Give the father a cask of Rhine wine and name no price
Offer a mark and a half
The bride-ale on the mound

Her kin stand in a ring on the mound, father's side and mother's. The price is to be counted where they can see it, her hand given, and the ale drunk. Her brother has brought his boat round on the tide.
Here are her kin, both sides. Count it out where they can see. Then I put her hand in yours and you take her home, and it is done before these people and before God.
A pound of pennies, as we said. I have counted the witnesses. Now I count the pennies.
You asked badly when you first came, and I made you wait for it. The waiting was the fine. The price is still a pound.
You promised black stones. I have looked in your boat. A man who forgets a promise to the uncle will forget one to the niece. Come back with them.

Those are Rhine stones in your boat. My wife has seen them. So has every wife on the mound. If they are a gift and not for sale, there is room under my roof for your goods for as long as I have a roof.
No church stands on the mound. A priest has walked a day over the marsh to bless what the kin have already settled, and to see that it is done in the open.
If you are my sister's man, my boat and yours can lie on the same bank. I know the Vlie and the flats. You know the Rhine. Between us that is the whole road.
The bolts in the chest are mine, and they go with me, not with the price. Sell them where cloth is short. Not here, where every hut has a loom.
The cloth in the chest is mine. Father will tell you how much there is. I will tell you if he is wrong.
Count out a pound of pennies before the kin
Count out the pound, and set down two pairs of black stones for the uncle as a gift
Ask for one more season
The deed and the blessing

At the door of Saint Martin's the dower is read out before the bishop's people, the earnest is laid in her father's hand, and a priest blesses the pair. The bishop has given his leave, on a condition.

It is written: to her, if she outlives him, a pound of silver as dower, a third of all they gain together, and whatever he gives her on the morning after. Witnesses, look at it. You need not read it. Look at it.
By our law a bride is pledged with a shilling and a penny, laid in my hand before these men. The dower goes into her own chest today, and I will watch it go in.
The bishop gives leave on one condition. The house you take her to stands under Saint Martin, as mine does: a pound of wax at his feast each year, and his letters carried when he asks.
For that you have a plot on his bank at Dorestad, no bank due is asked of you, and the count's men do not lodge under your roof.

Refuse, and she is still yours; the bishop will not stop a lawful marriage over a pound of wax. Then you deal with the count as before, and I keep a corner of my storehouse inside these walls for your goods.
Take the condition or leave it. But have it written that the storehouse keys are mine while you are at sea. I have kept my father's since my mother died, and he has lost nothing.
I have read it. It is fair. The clerk spelled my name two ways; I have made him choose.
People have come down from both churches to watch. A wedding in the open is the law. It is also the only thing happening in Traiectum today.
Give the earnest, fill her chest, and take Saint Martin's condition
Give the earnest and fill her chest, but keep your house the count's
Ask for one more season
The peace-weaving

Her kin and the archbishop's man stand witness in the wic by the Foss. You are to say before them how you will keep her, what you give for her, and what is hers if she outlives you, and your sureties must be named. The dead man is named first.
Before anything, I name my brother, who was killed here by a Frisian and is not paid for. Now everyone has heard it, and we can go on.
Before anything, I name my brother, who was killed here by a Frisian and paid for at last. Now everyone has heard it, and we can go on.

He is to promise, and his friends go surety, that he will keep her by God's law as a man should keep his wife. Then he names what he gives for her rearing, what he grants her for taking him, and what is hers if she outlives him.
entries.source: after 'Be wifmannes beweddunge' 1-4 (c. 1000-1030; Thorpe 1840), not re-read (?)

entries.text: And since he takes her out of this land into another, her kin must be sure that no wrong will be done her there.
entries.source: after 'Be wifmannes beweddunge' 7 (c. 1000-1030; Thorpe 1840), not re-read (?)

entries.text: You told me the worst thing first, in my own hall. My kin argued for a hundred nights. The women won. A pound and a half, and a plot by the Foss beside mine, where I can see what a Frisian does with it. Whoever touches your house here touches mine.
You let me learn from a wharf-hand whose silver is behind you. I learned it. Two pounds, and be glad it is a price. You may build by the Foss. I will not have my niece's man sleeping on the strand.
You are a stranger, and a stranger pays a stranger's price. Two pounds. You may build by the Foss. I will not have my niece's man sleeping on the strand.
Or the archbishop's man holds a pound for a year and a day. If she is well kept, it comes to her. If not, it comes to me, and so do you.
The old song I gave you says of every grief: that passed over, and so may this. A monk is not supposed to like such songs. I gave it to you so that I need not keep it.
entries.source: the refrain of Deor (texts_793.json deor), our rendering of the Old English

entries.text: Let my first son have my father's name. Then he will have come home, and my uncle can stop counting.
I have been told what you are. I have not been told who. I suppose there will be time.
Your steersman has not left the boat. From the strand he can be seen in the stern, sitting very still, facing the river.
Promise her first son the dead man's name, and count out a pound and a half
Count out two pounds and name your sureties
Lay a pound in the archbishop's man's hand for a year and a day
Ask for one more season
The handclasp

Witnesses stand round the host's fire at Ripa. The silver is to be weighed, hands clasped on the bargain, and the bridal ale drunk. Then there is the question of whose gods bless it, and what the priest at home will be told.

Here is my hand. Two marks for her. From this house she takes a chest, a loom, and my name behind her on this coast. You may build on my plot by the river and lie at my landing as a son does. Say it back before these men.
You offered me a mark and a half for my daughter. I have told that story at every fire since. It has been worth the other half-mark to me.
The twigs fell well twice and badly once. The bad one was water. Keep her off the sea in the dark of the year.
Now the hammer is laid in the bride's lap and she is hallowed, as the old song says it was done among the gods. Your god's man may stand outside for that part, if his god minds.
entries.source: after Thrymskvitha 30 (the manuscript is of about 1270: LATER) (?)

entries.text: My guests tell me your priests call a marriage with one of us no marriage. Ours say the same of yours. So we are even. What you tell your priest is your affair. What is done to my daughter's gods is mine.
Do right by her and by them, and any man of mine on this coast answers for your boat as he would for my own.
At Dorestad the priest will ask whether she has been to the font. The bishops forbid a Christian to wed a heathen. Nobody at Ripa has heard of the bishops.
I will hear your priest out, as a guest hears a host. If he wants to mark me with his cross for that, he may. It is a courtesy. It is not a washing.
My gods come with the chest. Stow them where you like, so long as it is dry.
Weigh out two marks, clasp hands, and let her gods come with her
Weigh out two marks, and ask her to take the sign of the cross as a guest
Pay in Frankish goods: three casks of wine and a crate of glass
Ask for one more season
The morning gift

On the morning after, a husband gives his wife a gift that is hers alone, whatever becomes of him. Every people on this sea has the custom and a word for it. What you give now is what she has if the sea keeps you.
Her kin are waiting outside to hear what it is. They will remember it longer than they remember the price.
Among us it need not be much. It must be mine.
It goes into the deed, under the dower. I will see that it does.
By the old law, if I bear no child, my father's kin have it back. So give me something worth their sailing for.
My mother had a cow and a kettle. She still has the kettle.
The keys of the house, and a third of all you gain together
Sixty pennies in a purse of her own
A pair of brooches from the hold
The keel comes home
A year on. The boat lies at the dam and there is a light in the house. The English have a verse about a Frisian's wife and her man's ship, and for once it is about you.

Dear is the welcome guest to the Frisian wife, when the vessel stands, his ship is come, and her husband to home, her own provider, and she calls him in, washes his weedy garment, and to him gives new raiment; 'tis pleasant on land to him whom his love awaits.
entries.source: Exeter Book, Gnomic Verses (Maxims I), tr. Benjamin Thorpe, Codex Exoniensis (London 1842), p. 339. Public domain.

entries.text: Her cloth is sold before it is off the loom, and her brother's boat has lain here beside yours. The dam says you married sheep. The dam is jealous.
She has read every tally in the house and found two of mine short. I like her. The count's man came for the bank due, looked at Saint Martin's mark on your post, and went away again.
She has read every tally in the house and found two of mine short. I like her. The count's man still comes for the bank due. She makes him wait while she counts it.
A ship of ours lay at Eoforwic all summer and nobody ran. My husband's name was said aloud there and no one reached for a knife. I did not think I would live to tell you that.
She weighs every penny that crosses your threshold, and has caught the moneyer's boy twice. Half the dam is afraid of her. The other half owes her.
She has not come to the font. I have not written to the bishop. Yet. Bring her to stand at the back at Easter, and I can go on not writing.
She let me sign her with the cross, and has stood at the back ever since. She asks hard questions about the bread. I count her a hearer. The bishop need not count at all.
She has held the keys while you were at sea. The storehouse is fuller than you left it, and she has the tally that says whose doing that was.
There is a cradle by the hearth. The widow says the child has your father's nose, and that this is not the child's fault.
Go in
Go in, and count what she has made of her third
First take the widow sixty pennies for her trouble

Evening at a dam head in Dorestad, low sun on the river: a Frisian widow of about forty in a white head-cloth, keys at her belt, has stopped a young skipper beside his small clinker boat; wattle and thatch storehouses on the dam behind them.

Inside the widow's storehouse on the dam, rain outside, one tallow light: she lays four tally sticks in a row on the head of a wine cask, one for each house, while the merchant stands with his cloak still wet.

A dry bright morning outside a small wooden church at Dorestad: the widow splits a notched tally stick down its length and holds out one half, while a priest sitting on the step writes on a scrap of parchment laid on his knee.

At sea under a grey sky, the small boat running before a light wind: the steersman at the side rudder looks straight ahead and says nothing, the mate grins from the oar bench, one ale cask lashed amidships.

A sod house mound above a flat salt marsh at Winaldum, wide sky, late afternoon sun: two older men on a bench by the door, the merchant standing before them, and in the dark mouth of a sunken hut a young woman at an upright loom, her hand still on the shuttle; sheep on the slope.

A timber hall inside old Roman stone walls at Traiectum, daylight from the open door: the bishop's steward at a trestle table, a priest with a wax tablet at his elbow, the daughter pouring ale from a black jug and looking at the merchant over it.

A Northumbrian hall at Eoforwic, noon light slanting through hearth smoke: a tall thegn in a dark red cloak with his hand near his sword hilt, a monk at his side, the Frisian merchant standing alone on the open floor, and a young woman among the women at the back, watching him.

A longhouse at Ripa at dusk, the long fire burning: the Danish host on his bench, an old woman laying three marked twigs on a white cloth, and in the doorway against the evening sky his daughter with folding scales, a small heap of cut silver in one pan.

The top of the mound at Winaldum on a windy bright day: kin standing in a ring, pennies being counted onto a cloth in the middle, the bride with her hand in her father's, a priest muddy to the knee from the marsh, and a second boat drawn up on the creek bank below.

The door of Saint Martin's inside the fort at Traiectum on a still grey morning: a priest reads from a parchment, the steward holds out his open hand for a shilling and a penny, the bride stands beside a small iron-bound chest, and the bishop's people look on from the yard.

The strand by the Foss at Eoforwic under a cold clear sky: the kin in a half circle, the thegn speaking with one hand raised, a monk and the archbishop's man as witnesses, the bride in a cloak pinned with a silver ring; out on the river the Frisian boat, with one man sitting very still in her stern.

Night in the host's house at Ripa, firelight on faces: the Dane and the merchant clasp hands over a pair of scales heaped with silver, witnesses standing round, the bride seated with a small iron hammer laid in her lap and the old woman behind her.

Early morning, pale light through an open door: the new wife sits on the edge of the bed with a married woman's head-cloth on for the first time; the merchant holds out a ring of keys, and a small purse and a pair of brooches lie on the chest between them.

Dusk at the dam at Dorestad a year later, light rain: the small boat made fast, a lit doorway up the bank with a woman in it holding a child, dry clothes over her arm; the widow under her storehouse eave, watching, pleased with herself.
